title: SOPs: Cleaning, Guest Communication & Emergency Response

slides.title: Write each routine so a backup can run it from the driveway without calling you
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.8. SOPs: Cleaning, Guest Communication & Emergency Response
meta: Education only. Not legal, fire safety, or insurance advice. In an emergency, call 911.
slides.notes:
After this lesson you'll have a short operating playbook for your house. A backup cleaner or a new co-host can follow it without calling you.

It has three pieces. The first is a turnover checklist with photo proof, par levels for supplies, and an escalation ladder for a missed clean. The second is a message sequence, with a named owner for every message. The third is an emergency matrix for seven kinds of incident.

Then we'll run all of it at Cedar Ridge three times. There's a normal Sunday turnover. There's a guest problem on a Tuesday, when the internet goes down during a work stay. And there's a real emergency at 1:40 in the morning, when the CO alarm sounds.

The people in these SOPs come from OP.7. The cleaner has calendar access. The handyman takes the after-hours calls. Maya owns guest messaging, and Chris backs her up. If you haven't built your role map yet, do that first. An SOP without a named owner isn't finished.

slides.title: A usable SOP names a trigger, one owner, a standard, proof, escalation, and a record
items: Trigger: what starts it (a checkout, a message, an alarm)
Owner: one named role from the OP.7 role map
Steps, in order
Standard: what "done" looks like, specifically
Proof: a photo, a timestamp, or a reading
Escalation and record: who to call by when if a step fails, and where the result is written

box.label: One page each
box.text: If an SOP runs longer than a page, split it. The backup cleaner reads it in the driveway, not at a desk.

slides.notes:
A standard operating procedure, or SOP, is a written routine that gives the same result no matter who follows it. Most short-term rental checklists fail that test. They say "clean kitchen" and leave the standard to the cleaner's mood that day.

Every SOP in this lesson has seven parts. I've put the last two on one line to fit the slide, but they're separate: escalation, then record.

The trigger is what starts it. The owner is one named role, taken from your OP.7 role map. One role, not "the team." The standard says what done looks like, specifically enough that two people would agree. The proof is a photo, a timestamp, or a reading. Escalation says who to call, and by when, if a step fails. The record says where the result gets written down.

Keep each one to a page. The person using it is standing in a driveway with a phone, often on the day they're covering for someone else.

slides.title: The turnover starts with a walk-through before anything is touched, so damage is on camera
slides.keyline: Trigger: checkout in the calendar. Owner: turnover cleaner. Window: 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. (assumption).
rows: Start time recorded in the task app
Damage, missing items, smoke smell, signs of extra guests, items left behind
All 6 beds stripped, used or not
Dishes put away, appliances wiped, fridge emptied, trash out
Toilets, showers, sinks, mirrors, floors; hair check on every surface
Beds made in the standard set, surfaces dusted, under beds checked
slides.notes:
The turnover runs more than any other SOP. At Cedar Ridge's base case, it runs 61 times a year. Airbnb's ground rules for hosts set cleanliness as an expectation. Hosts should clean between every stay: laundry, trash, vacuuming or sweeping, and wiping surfaces. Your SOP turns that into a standard.

The trigger is the checkout in the calendar. The owner is the turnover cleaner, who has calendar access only, per OP.7. The window is six hours, from a 10 a.m. checkout to a 4 p.m. check-in.

Step two is the one I care about most. The cleaner walks the house before touching anything. They note damage, missing items, a smoke smell, signs of extra guests, and anything left behind. Damage gets photographed before cleaning, because after cleaning, the evidence is gone.

Step three strips all six beds, whether they were used or not. That keeps the linen cycle simple and nobody has to guess which beds were slept in.

slides.title: The last six steps check safety and send photos the owner reviews from two hours away
rows: Surfaces, cushions, remotes, floors vacuumed or mopped
Furniture set, grill grates clean, cover on, no guest trash
Alarms present and not disabled; extinguishers in place; no indoor device; owner closet locked
Each alarm location, weekly test logged
Lights off, thermostat to vacancy setting, doors locked
Checklist complete; damage and low stock flagged

box.label: Alarms
box.text: Airbnb says alarms that are present must work and be tested regularly. The turnover checks none were removed. The full button test goes in the monthly inspection.

slides.notes:
Photos serve two purposes. Maya and Chris live about two hours away, so the photos let them check the work without driving there. And the photos are evidence if a guest later reports a problem. The retained lesson 9.3 Dealing With Damages covers how to use damage photos in a claim.

Step 10 is the safety check. Airbnb's safety requirements say that if smoke and CO alarms are present, hosts must keep them working and test them regularly. So at every turnover, the cleaner checks that no alarm has been removed or disabled.

The full button test is a separate job. It goes in the monthly inspection, which belongs to the handyman. Set the test schedule using the alarm manufacturer's instructions and your fire marshal's advice.

Step 12 is the report. The checklist is complete, damage and low stock are flagged, and every photo is uploaded. Maya reviews the photos before the check-in message goes out.

slides.title: Keep four stays of supplies on site and reorder when the shelf drops to two
slides.text: Consumables run about $25 per stay, $1,525 a year across 61 stays. Four stays on hand is about $100 of stock (assumption). Linens follow the OP.6 cycle: 18 sheet sets, 24 towel sets.
rows: Coffee, tea, sugar, oil, salt, pepper
slides.notes:
Par level means the amount you keep on hand. The reorder point is when someone orders more. Write both numbers on the shelf label, so nobody has to guess.

At Cedar Ridge, consumables run about $25 per stay. That's $1,525 a year across 61 stays. Keeping stock for four stays on site is about $100 worth. Reorder at two. That leaves room for a back-to-back weekend without a supply run.

Linens follow the OP.6 cycle. There are 18 sheet sets, three per bed for six beds. There are 24 towel sets, three per guest for eight guests. One set is on each bed, one is in the laundry, and one is on the shelf. The cleaner counts the shelf at every turnover. If any bed has fewer than one clean set on the shelf after the beds are made, the cleaner flags it.

Replacements follow the approval limits from OP.6 and OP.7. A broken glass comes from the spares shelf and gets noted. Anything over $200 needs owner approval first.

slides.title: The missed-clean ladder catches a no-show by 11 a.m., not at 3:30 p.m.
rows: Cleaner confirms in the task app
Call; no answer in 15 minutes, send the backup
Warn the guest; offer a later check-in
Delay check-in, or send a second cleaner
Owner reviews photos before releasing the code
Second miss in 90 days triggers a scope review

box.label: What the backup costs
box.text: Same-day premium: $200 instead of $150 (assumption). Four times a year: 4 × $50 = $200 more. Cheap next to a refund and a one-star cleanliness review.

slides.notes:
The worst operational failure is a guest arriving to a dirty house. It usually starts with a cleaner who doesn't show up and a host who finds out at 3:30 in the afternoon.

The ladder catches it by late morning. The night before, the cleaner confirms in the task app by 8 p.m. If not, Maya calls. If there's still no confirmation by 9, the backup cleaner gets asked to hold the slot.

On the day, the arrival photo should be in by 11. If it isn't, Maya calls the cleaner. No answer in 15 minutes, and the backup goes.

At 2:30 she counts photos. If the turnover isn't half done, she decides whether to delay check-in or send a second cleaner. At 3:45, she reviews the final photos before the door code goes out.

The backup is paid a same-day premium, $200 instead of $150. If that happens four times a year, it costs $200 more. That's cheap next to a refund and a one-star cleanliness review.

slides.title: Every guest gets the same seven messages, and a named person checks each one
rows: Thanks, what to expect, house rules, guest count check
Correct guest count and no-party rule
Directions, parking, lake access rules, what to bring
Address, door code, Wi-Fi, house manual
Correct unique code for this stay
Sent by someone who can act
Offer a restock or answer questions
slides.caption: Maya owns and checks every message. Every Monday she reviews the week's scheduled messages against each booking: guest count, dates, lock code, special arrangements.
slides.notes:
Every guest gets the same core messages at the same moments. Automation sends most of them. A named person owns each one and checks it. At Cedar Ridge, that's Maya for all seven.

Airbnb lets hosts send scheduled quick replies automatically. They're triggered by events like a new booking, check-in, or checkout. The same help page says you can skip, send early, or edit an upcoming message without changing the template. When you host with a team, members with guest management permissions share the scheduled replies, and messages go out from the team owner.

Look at the day-before message. It carries the door code, so it's held for review. A wrong code in a scheduled message means a family standing on the porch at 4 p.m.

The check-in evening message is manual on purpose. It has to come from someone who can act on the answer.

And human review is a written weekly step. Every Monday, Maya opens the list of scheduled messages for the week and checks each one against the booking.

slides.title: No bot answers a message about smoke, gas, leaks, injury, lockouts, or refunds
items: A person answers anything about smoke, fire, gas, alarms, leaks, injury, police, lockouts, or refunds, immediately
No automated message sends a changed door code; a person sends it after checking the lock
An AI suggestion is a draft; a person approves it, unless it's an approved template for a routine question
Any exception granted (early check-in, late checkout, extra guest) goes in the booking notes so the cleaner sees it

box.label: Where this connects
box.text: SR.5 compares AI messaging tools on these criteria. Sam's OP.4 shows where messages and tasks live in the tech stack.

slides.notes:
Automation needs limits. Write these into the SOP and into the settings of any AI messaging tool you use.

The first limit is the important one. No automated or AI reply goes to a message about smoke, fire, gas, alarms, leaks, injury, police, lockouts, or refunds. A person answers those, immediately. A friendly auto-reply to "the CO alarm is going off" is the worst message you could send.

Second, no automated message sends a changed door code. A person checks the lock first, then sends it.

Third, an AI suggestion is a draft. Airbnb offers suggested quick replies that use AI to pick one of your existing replies for common questions. A person approves the suggestion before it goes, unless it's an approved template for a routine question.

Fourth, any exception you grant goes in the booking notes. If Maya allows a late checkout, the cleaner needs to see it.

From Sam's OP.4 lesson, bring back where your messages and tasks actually run, so you can set these limits in the right place.

slides.title: The emergency matrix says what to do first, who responds, and who can stop work
rows: Get everyone out, then call 911 from outside
911; after-hours contact to site; owner told
Everyone out to fresh air, then call 911
911 or fire dept; gas utility; licensed HVAC
Anyone; no re-entry until fire dept clears it
Shut off water at the main; avoid electrical
Call or message the on-call number
Messaging owner resets code; handyman if lock fails
911 for anything serious; first aid kit in manual
Owner decides if area stays closed
Check the utility's outage page or manual steps
Follow official warnings; shelter in manual
slides.caption: Record every incident: times, photos, report numbers, insurer notice. Airbnb: call local emergency services first.
slides.notes:
An emergency matrix tells the person on the spot what to do first and who to call. It also says who can stop work and what to record. Write it for the guest and the team together. The guest's part goes in the house manual.

Airbnb's help center says to contact local emergency services first if an emergency is in progress. Airbnb also describes an Urgent Support Line in its app for hosts and guests during active reservations. Neither one replaces 911. Neither one replaces your own on-call person.

Read the first action column. For fire and CO, it's the same shape: get out first, then call. Nobody investigates a CO alarm from inside the house.

For a leak, the first action depends on the guest knowing where the water main is. So the shutoff location gets marked in the manual.

Every incident gets a record: times, photos, report numbers, and an insurer notice when there's damage or injury. The fire department and the insurer should confirm these steps for your house.

slides.title: Anyone can stop work for safety, but only an owner reopens the calendar

left.head: Stop-work authority
items: The right to halt a turnover, a repair, or the next booking because something isn't safe
At Cedar Ridge, anyone on the team can use it
Only an owner reopens the calendar
And only after the right professional signs off

right.head: Laminated contact sheet
right.note: Inside the owner closet door, with a copy in the house manual
items: 911, non-emergency police and fire
Utilities and the water shutoff location
On-call phone, handyman, plumber, HVAC company
Insurer's claim line; fill in real numbers before the first booking

slides.notes:
Stop-work authority means the right to halt a turnover, a repair, or the next booking because something isn't safe.

At Cedar Ridge, anyone on the team can stop work for safety. The cleaner can. The handyman can. Nobody needs permission to say "this isn't safe, we stop."

Reopening works the other way. Only an owner can reopen the calendar, and only after the right professional signs off. After a CO alarm, that's the fire department, the HVAC technician, and the gas supplier. Stopping is easy on purpose. Restarting is hard on purpose.

The contact sheet is the other half. It's laminated and kept inside the owner closet door, with a copy in the house manual. It lists 911 and the non-emergency police and fire numbers. It lists the utilities and where the water shutoff is. It lists the on-call phone, the handyman, the plumber, the HVAC company, and the insurer's claim line.

Fill in the real local numbers before the first booking. A blank line on that sheet at 2 a.m. costs time.

slides.title: Privacy rules go in the SOPs, because well-meaning people are the ones who break them
slides.text: Airbnb bans indoor cameras and recording devices, even if off. Exterior cameras must be disclosed. Noise monitors that don't record are allowed in disclosed common spaces only.
items: Turnover: no new device has appeared indoors
Turnover: the noise monitor is still in its disclosed common-area spot
Turnover: the doorbell camera still points only at the entry
Data: camera footage and guest details stay in the platform or the device's own app
Data: nobody downloads them to a personal phone or shares them outside the team
slides.notes:
Privacy rules belong in the SOPs, because the people who break them usually mean well. A cleaner might want to set up a "nanny cam" to watch for parties. That's not allowed.

Airbnb's device rules prohibit security cameras and recording devices that monitor indoor spaces, even if they're off. Exterior cameras have to be disclosed in the listing. They can't watch indoor spaces or areas like an enclosed outdoor shower. Noise decibel monitors that don't record sound are allowed in common spaces if they're disclosed. They're not allowed in bedrooms, bathrooms, or sleeping areas.

So I put three lines in the turnover SOP and two lines in the data SOP. They're on the slide. The cleaner checks the devices every turnover, the same way they check the alarms.

The data lines matter because footage and guest details are easy to copy. They stay in the platform or the device's own app.

The retained lesson 9.4 How to Avoid Parties & Smoking covers the party-prevention side.

slides.title: A normal Sunday turnover finishes by 2:20 p.m. and leaves six clean sets on the shelf

lines.label: Clean sets put on the 6 beds
Used sets sent to the wash

result.label: Clean sets left on the shelf

slides.side:
10:25 a.m. arrival photo; walk-through finds a chipped mug and a stained lake towel.

1:55 p.m. restock: supplies drop from four stays to three, above the reorder point of two.

2:00 p.m. mug and towel replaced from spares and logged; under $200, no approval.

2:45 p.m. Maya reviews photos and releases the check-in message. Cleaner pay $150; cleaning fee $175.
slides.notes:
Now the three walk-throughs. The first is a normal Sunday. A family of seven checks out at 10 a.m. after a 3.5-night stay. The next group of eight arrives at 4.

The cleaner confirmed at 8:05 the night before. The arrival photo comes in at 10:25. The walk-through finds one chipped mug and a lake towel with a stain.

By 10:40, all six beds are stripped and laundry has started. Six clean sets go on the beds, six used sets go to the wash. Eighteen minus six minus six leaves six clean sets on the shelf. That's one per bed, so no flag.

Cleaning runs about three hours. At 1:55 the restock drops supplies from four stays to three, still above the reorder point. The mug is replaced from the spares shelf and the towel goes to the rag bin. It's under $200, so no approval is needed.

Final photos go up at 2:20. Maya reviews them at 2:45 and releases the check-in message. The cleaner earned $150. The guest paid a $175 cleaning fee.

slides.title: When the internet fails, give facts, a credit, and a fix, and leave reviews out of it
slides.text: Tuesday, four-night midweek stay. The listing advertises a dedicated workspace.

nodes.d: No safety words, so an auto-acknowledgment is allowed. A person must reply within 30 minutes.
Maya sends the house manual steps: unplug the router 30 seconds, wait five minutes
Area outage, fix estimated by 6 p.m. No guessing at a restore time
Inside her OP.7 limit, through the platform, not tied to a review
Record times, provider reference, credit, and a root-cause note

box.label: Root cause
box.text: An advertised workspace on one internet line has no backup. Chris gets a quote for a cellular backup router. It's over $200, so it goes on the owner decision list for month end.

slides.notes:
The second walk-through is a guest problem. On a Tuesday, a guest on a four-night stay messages at 9:05: "Internet is down. I have work calls today." And the listing advertises a dedicated workspace.

The message has no safety words, so an automated acknowledgment is allowed. The SOP still requires a person within 30 minutes. Maya replies at 9:15 with the reset steps from the house manual.

At 9:35 it's still down. Maya checks the provider's outage page. It shows an area outage, with a fix estimated by 6 p.m. At 9:40 she tells the guest what she knows and when she'll update them. She doesn't guess at a time the provider hasn't given.

At 10 she offers a $100 goodwill credit. That's inside her OP.7 limit. She pays it through the platform, not in cash. And she doesn't tie it to a review, because Airbnb's review policy prohibits offering something of value for a review. OP.9 covers that.

Service returns at 6:20. Then comes the useful part, the root-cause note.

slides.title: At 1:40 a.m. the CO alarm sounds, and everyone is outside before anyone investigates
rows: "Get everyone outside now, then call 911." Stays on the line until all eight are out
Handyman drives over (about 35 minutes); doesn't go inside
Fire department finds elevated CO near the propane furnace, shuts off gas
Uses Airbnb's urgent support; books a hotel as an emergency exception
"Do not occupy" notice on the door; next arrival blocked
Licensed HVAC inspection; closed until tech and gas supplier clear it in writing
Incident report, report number, findings, receipts; insurer notified
slides.notes:
The third walk-through is a real emergency. It's 1:40 on a Saturday morning. A guest calls the after-hours number because the CO alarm on the lower level is sounding.

The handyman answers, per the OP.7 after-hours row. His first words come straight from the matrix: get everyone outside now, then call 911. He stays on the line until all eight guests are out.

He drives over, about 35 minutes, but he doesn't go inside. The fire department controls the scene. They find elevated CO near the furnace, which in this example is propane, and shut off the gas.

Relocation costs more than anyone on the team is allowed to spend. So Chris authorizes it himself as an emergency exception and books a hotel.

At 2:30 it's stop-work. A notice goes on the door and the next arrival is blocked. The house stays closed until the HVAC technician and the gas supplier clear it in writing. Chris notifies the insurer the same day. The monthly inspection now adds a furnace service check before each heating season.

slides.title: Fill in your emergency matrix with real local numbers, and date each one
slides.caption: Also fill in one SOP header per routine: name, trigger, owner, backup, steps, standard, proof, escalation, record, last reviewed.
slides.notes:
The exercise has two parts. The first is an SOP header for every routine. Name, trigger, owner, backup, numbered steps, the standard for done, the proof required, the escalation, the record, and the date it was last reviewed. One page per SOP.

The second part is on the slide: your own emergency matrix. Don't copy Cedar Ridge's numbers, because they aren't real. Look up the real local ones.

Write the water shutoff location right in the row. Write the shelter location for severe weather right in the row. Those are the two things a guest can't find in the dark.

The last column is the date you verified each number. Phone numbers change. Vendors change. A number you checked two years ago might ring a stranger.

For fire and CO, the first action is already set: get out, then call 911. What you're filling in is who responds after that, with names and phones, and who has stop-work authority. Ask the fire department to look at those two rows with you.

slides.title: Four checks tell you whether your SOPs are finished or still drafts

gates.q: Does every step have a named owner?
Has the backup done the SOP once, for real or in a paid trial?
Can an automated message send a door code or reply to a safety message?
gates.sub: Here the safe answer is no.
gates.no: If yes, change the setting before the next booking

gates.q: Has every SOP been reviewed after the last incident and within six months (assumption)?

slides.end: All four pass: the house runs the same way whoever is on duty.
slides.notes:
These four checks come from the lesson's decision rules. Run them before your first booking, and again after any incident.

First, every step needs a named owner. If a step says "someone checks the alarms," it isn't finished. Put the role there.

Second, a backup has to have done the SOP once, for real or in a paid trial. A name on a list isn't a backup. A person who has already walked your house with the checklist is.

Third, look at your messaging settings. Can any automated message send a door code? Can one reply to a message about smoke or a leak? The safe answer there is no. If it's yes, change the setting before the next booking.

Fourth, review every SOP after any incident, and at least every six months. The six months is an assumption, so pick your own interval. At Cedar Ridge, the CO incident added a furnace check before heating season. That's what a review is for.

slides.title: The fire department, insurer, and utilities confirm the emergency side of your SOPs
rows: First actions for fire and CO alarms at this house, and alarm testing frequency
Incident notice deadlines, required records, and whether relocation costs are covered
Scheduled messages, safety requirements, and device rules, checked before recording
slides.notes:
The emergency parts of these SOPs need outside confirmation.

The local fire department confirms the first actions for fire and CO alarms at your house. Ask them how often alarms should be tested, too. What I've shown you follows Airbnb's guidance to call emergency services first. The fire department sets the specifics.

The insurer confirms how fast they need incident notice and what records they want. Ask whether relocation costs are covered. In the Cedar Ridge emergency, Chris booked a hotel at 2:15 in the morning. He should already know whether that's covered before it happens.

The utilities confirm emergency numbers and shutoff procedures. That includes gas or propane, electric, and water. The propane supplier is the one who clears the furnace in the example.

And check Airbnb's current pages on scheduled messages, safety requirements, and device rules before you rely on them. These pages change.

slides.title: This week, write the turnover SOP and fill in the real emergency numbers
items: Write your turnover SOP on one page, with a photo proof column and the cleaner named as owner.
Find and label your water main shutoff, then add its location to the house manual.
Fill in the emergency matrix with real local numbers and today's date beside each one.
Open your messaging settings and make sure no automated message sends a door code or answers a safety message.
slides.next: Next: OP.9 Guest Experience & Review Strategy in the AI Ranking Era. It connects these SOPs to what Airbnb publishes about search and reviews.
slides.notes:
Four actions, each under an hour.

Write the turnover SOP on one page. Use the twelve steps as a starting point, but make the standards fit your house. Add the photo proof column and name the owner.

Go find your water main shutoff. Put a label on it. Add its location to the house manual and the contact sheet.

Fill in the emergency matrix with real local numbers, and write today's date next to each.

Then open your messaging settings. Check that nothing automated sends a door code or replies to a safety message.

The house now runs the same way whether Maya, Chris, or a backup is on duty. The next question is how guests experience that work, and what they say about it afterward. OP.9 connects these SOPs to what Airbnb publishes about search. It also shows how to ask for reviews within Airbnb's rules and how to track what guests tell you.

box.label: Cedar Ridge figures
box.text: From the canonical file, B1: 61 stays, cleaner $150, cleaning fee $175, supplies $1,525. Par levels, times, and premiums are assumptions.

slides.notes:
Six Airbnb pages back the platform rules in these SOPs. I checked all of them on 2026-09-25 through search summaries.

The ground rules page covers cleaning between every stay and the communication expectations. The safety requirements page covers alarm disclosure, keeping alarms working, and regular testing. The device page covers the indoor camera ban, exterior camera disclosure, and noise monitors.

The scheduled quick replies page covers message triggers, skipping or editing an upcoming message, team sharing, and AI-suggested replies. The community safety page says to contact local emergency services first. The newsroom post describes the Urgent Support Line in the app.

The Cedar Ridge figures come from section B1 of the canonical example: 61 stays, a $150 cleaner, a $175 cleaning fee, and $1,525 in supplies. The par levels, the times in the walk-throughs, and the backup premium are teaching assumptions.

Nothing here replaces your fire department or your insurer. They confirm the emergency steps for your house.
